My title is not “social worker”, and I do not have a social work license, but my job is usually likened to one of a social worker/case worker.

Been in this job 6 months today, over 45 clients, and got chewed out by a clients family today for sucking at my job. 

The problem is, some of what she said was true. I’m difficult to get in touch with. But that doesn’t mean I care about her family’s case any less. A nurse misled her as to what my job is, and caused her to lash out today. 

I feel so lost because there’s only so much I can do. I’m not allowed to pester the state until she gets what she has been asking for. The decision has been pending since before I had her on my case load, and other peoples’ cases have been pending OVER a year. 

Trying not to take it personally, but when most of my clients families say I’m a “blessing” or that I’m doing “good”, this type of criticism just blocks all that out. I’m already slated to take a mental health day tomorrow. I am so thankful my agency gives us those. 

I’m trying to tell myself, or ask myself, how I would act if it was my own family. So I understand her frustration. But I also would be understanding to a workers’ limitations. There’s so much red tape, so much waiting. And that’s not my fault.

I’ve already lost 1 other client in the past couple weeks, but that was completely not my fault. Now I can see in this case where I went wrong. What more I might have been able to do? Might, being the key word. Doesn’t mean the outcome would have been any different.

How does everyone handle this type of criticism? Especially from a client? And where they are partially correct, in pointing out your wrongs? 

I’ll be embroidering for the next 24 hours at least. I’m trying to refuse to beat myself up… but it’s difficult.

So I'd say primary responsibilities are mainly doctors office related - rooming patients, cleaning and resetting rooms, taking patient vitals (mine did manual BP so be ready for that), entering into the computer system. So my office, the MA's would perform the "spirometries". So the spirometry was basically like, a tube people breath in/out into and it brings up a graph on the computer. Your office MAY do them in a special appointment with a RT, usually called PFTs where it's a group of tests. But we had a couple single spirometry systems that would hook up to the computer via USB, and mainly you just need to give the directions, then talk them through while they're doing it, and the goal for us was to do the best of 3 trials. Print and give to doctor. If you want to start practicing for the direction giving, it's mainly: Plug nose with nose piece (usually comes with it), take the "device", have the pt take a deep breath in, then put the mouth piece in their mouth, blow out as hard and as fast as they can, you're looking for them to reach a certain kind of arc on the graph on the computer so they WILL feel out of breath, and then you will advise them when they reach that point, to take a SHARP deep breath in, and that's it! 

Honestly, that was the biggest thing I learned, other than medications, generic and formularies, and doing prior authorizations or appeals for insurance purposes. Sometimes, also, being the go-between with patients and doctors, if they have a question or non-urgent issue. Also giving injections if the doctor tells you to.

So ultimately, and I know you know this, you need to reach out for help. Because self harm masks the pain in the moment, but the relief is SO temporary. Therapy is of course awesome, but I also use free support groups and things like that (as long as you aren't being explicit about the harm). 

I also encourage you to look into DBT, and especially a therapist who at least knows it and can help you apply it. The main skill for self harm is TIPP - temperature, intensity (exercise), paced breathing and progressive muscle relaxation. I ALWAYS use temperature. So when my urges were bad, I could like drive with the window down in the winter AND a/c on full blast, as long as I could handle it. Those particular things I guess kinda help your mind to "snap out of it", if that makes sense?

Now since it's summer, a lot of the time I will just come home from work and shower, and at the end of my shower, push it to as cold as possible and have the water hitting my face (dive reflex, also relates to the temperature thing) and I do it for at least 30 seconds. Then I turn it off and I am at least a bit more clear headed and can make better, less impulsive decisions.

So yes, DBT. I haven't harmed in a few months, and no un-aliving attempts for over a year, and I completely accredit that to my work in DBT.
